extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, lawyers, and activists interested in U.S. First Amendment and free-speech doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the legal concept of the heckler's veto in U.S. law: its definitions, doctrinal tests, key Supreme Court holdings, and distinctions between colloquial and legal usages. Useful for understanding when government action (or private conduct) counts as a heckler's veto and related exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — heckler's veto (discourse)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the discourse, a heckler's veto is a situation in which a party who disagrees with a speaker's message is able to unilaterally trigger events that result in the speaker being silenced (for example, a heckler can disrupt a speech to the point that the speech is canceled).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: disruptive heckling that forces cancellation; colloquial usage often treats the heckler as the actor who directly silences the speaker. The article notes this common, non-legal understanding and gives disruption-as-cancellation as the typical example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal definition — government suppression because of anticipated reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: In the legal sense, a heckler's veto occurs when the speaker's right is curtailed or restricted by the government in order to prevent a reacting party's behavior; the common example is termination of a speech or demonstration in the interest of maintaining the public peace based on the anticipated negative reaction of someone opposed to that speech or demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crucial distinction: under First Amendment law it is the government's curtailment — prompted by the possibility of a violent reaction by hecklers — that constitutes a heckler's veto. The article emphasizes that this legal form of heckler's veto is unconstitutional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-emptive suppression disallowed; immediate-violence exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Most findings say that the acting party's actions cannot be pre-emptively stopped due to fear of heckling by the reacting party, but in the immediate face of violence, authorities can force the acting party to cease their action in order to satisfy the hecklers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets a rule-of-thumb: anticipated disturbance alone does not justify silencing the speaker (pre-emption is impermissible), while a present, immediate threat to safety may permit authorities to act to preserve order even if that results in curtailing the speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feiner v. New York standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Feiner v. New York (1951): Chief Justice Vinson held that police officers acted within their power in arresting a speaker if the arrest was 'motivated solely by a proper concern for the preservation of order and protection of the general welfare.' (340 U.S. 315).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Feiner as precedent where police conduct that interrupts speech may be upheld if genuinely aimed at preserving order and public safety — courts will examine the government's motive and immediacy of threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gregory v. City of Chicago perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: In Gregory v. Chicago (1969), Justice Hugo Black, in a concurring opinion, argued that arresting demonstrators as a consequence of unruly behavior of by-standers would amount to a heckler's veto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concurrence articulates the position that punishing or silencing speakers/demonstrators because of hostile bystanders' reactions effectively hands veto power to the hecklers; useful as a counterpoint to cases like Feiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hill v. Colorado — content-neutral regulation not a heckler's veto when message can be conveyed
rubrics_metrics.description: Hill v. Colorado (2000): the Supreme Court ruled a law forbidding protesters from approaching within eight feet of a person without consent was not a heckler's veto, because protesters could still convey their message across that gap; the law prevented physical harassment rather than speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: a regulation that restricts the manner of protest but leaves reasonable alternative channels to convey the message may not constitute a heckler's veto; conversely, the Court stated it would not uphold a law that 'allowed a single, private actor to unilaterally silence a speaker even as to willing listeners.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Schenck v. Pro-Choice Network — struck-down restriction that effectively silenced protesters
rubrics_metrics.description: Schenck v. Pro-Choice Network of Western New York (1997): the Court struck down a provision that would require anti-abortion protesters 'either to stop talking or to get off the sidewalk whenever a patient came within 15 feet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates that rules that effectively force speakers/protesters to stop communicating when listeners are present can be invalidated as creating a veto-like suppression of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mahanoy concurring analogy — school regulation as heckler's veto
rubrics_metrics.description: In a concurring opinion to Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L. (2021) dealing with regulation of off-campus student speech, Justice Samuel Alito likened the ability of schools attempting to punish students for speaking out against the school as a form of a heckler's veto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows extension of the concept into school-speech contexts: disciplining speakers in response to hostile reactions or political pressure can be characterized as a heckler's veto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colloquial versus legal usage distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside the strict legal context, heckler's veto is often used to mean the heckler themself is the party which directly carries out the 'veto' and suppresses speech. That plain-English interpretation differs from the legal meaning, which focuses on government suppression prompted by hecklers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing incidents or arguing cases, be careful to identify whether the suppression is primarily private (hecklers disrupting) or governmental (officials silencing speech because of hecklers) — only the latter is the classic constitutional 'heckler's veto'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative/legal principle — government may act to prevent a heckler's veto
rubrics_metrics.description: As articulated by commentators (e.g., Erwin Chemerinsky), 'The law is well established that the government can act to prevent a heckler’s veto – to prevent the reaction of the audience from silencing the speaker.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses the normative judicial and scholarly stance that authorities should protect speakers from being shouted down; enforcement must, however, respect First Amendment limits and not itself become content-based suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive label — 'verbal terrorism' as characterization of heckling tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Michigan State University professor William B. Allen has used the phrase 'verbal terrorism' to refer to the same phenomenon, defining it as 'calculated assault characterized by loud side-conversations, shouted interruptions, jabbered false facts, threats and personal insults.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a behavioral typology of disruptive conduct that courts and commentators may cite when assessing whether disruption is intended to and does in practice silence speakers.
